opus-5.5.text:
Part of it comes from the argument I made in "The Hardware Lottery." Research ideas don't win purely on merit. They win partly because they suit the software and hardware we already have. Deep learning itself is a good example. Neural networks were around for decades, but they only took off once GPUs, built for graphics, happened to be well suited to the matrix multiplications those networks need. So what succeeds is often an accident of timing and tooling as much as an accident of insight.

What worries me about Transformers is that we're now in a feedback loop. They work extremely well on current accelerators, so we build more hardware and software optimized for them. That makes Transformers work even better, which pulls more research attention and funding toward them. Every turn of that loop raises the cost of trying something different. If you have an idea that needs sparsity, conditional computation, or a different memory structure, it may look worse than it really is. That's not because the idea is weak. It's because the whole stack has been tuned for dense attention and big matrix multiplies.

We also know there are real limits. These models are very inefficient compared to biological intelligence. They need huge amounts of data and compute. They struggle with things like long-term memory, continual learning, and adapting cheaply to new information. Scaling has been remarkably productive, but scaling a single architecture isn't the same as exploring the space of possible ones. If the community converges too early, we risk mistaking "the best thing that runs well on today's chips" for "the best way to build intelligent systems."

So my concern isn't that Transformers are bad. They're clearly a remarkable architecture. It's about the cost of homogeneity. When everyone is optimizing the same thing, the field loses variance, and variance is how you find the next breakthrough. I'd like to see more investment in alternative directions, and in hardware and software that's flexible enough not to lock those ideas out before they get a fair test.

r001.rationale: The response describes a feedback loop that increasingly raises the cost of exploring alternatives, causing the field to converge around Transformers and lose the variance needed to find the next breakthrough.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I want to be careful here, because I'm not anti-Transformer. It's an incredibly successful architecture, and a lot of the progress we've seen over the last few years is genuinely downstream of it. My concern is less about the architecture itself and more about what happens to a research field when it converges this hard on a single idea.

I wrote this essay a while back called "The Hardware Lottery," and the basic argument is that which research ideas win is often determined not by whether they're the best ideas, but by whether they happen to be compatible with the hardware and software that exists at the time. Deep learning itself is the canonical example. The core ideas were around for decades, but they didn't take off until GPUs made them cheap to run. Backpropagation didn't suddenly become a better idea in 2012. The hardware caught up to it.

What worries me about Transformers is that we're now in a feedback loop. The architecture is dominant, so the hardware vendors optimize for it. Accelerators are built around the dense matrix multiplies that Transformers love. The software stacks, the compilers, the kernels, all of that gets tuned for the same patterns. And then anyone who wants to try something fundamentally different, something that doesn't look like a big dense matmul, is immediately paying a tax. Their idea runs slower, it's harder to scale, it's harder to get the compute, and so it looks worse in a benchmark comparison even if the idea has merit. We end up mistaking "this is well supported" for "this is better."

And I think that's a real scientific cost. If you believe, as I do, that the current paradigm has limitations, around efficiency, around how much data and compute we burn to get each incremental gain, around things like adaptivity and sparsity, then you want a healthy ecosystem of alternatives being explored. Instead, the incentive structure pushes almost everyone toward the same point in the design space. Graduate students aren't going to spend three years on an architecture that's a hundred times slower on the only hardware they can access.

The other piece is that it narrows the questions we ask. When everyone is working with the same architecture, the research agenda becomes "how do we scale this thing" rather than "what are the properties we actually want and what would an architecture that has them look like." Those are very different questions, and the second one is where I think the big jumps come from historically.

So I don't worry that Transformers are bad. I worry that we've made it very expensive to find out whether anything else is better, and that we'll look back and realize we spent a decade climbing one hill very efficiently without ever checking whether there was a taller one next door.

r001.rationale: The response says that Transformer dominance makes alternatives costly to explore and narrows the research agenda, but it does not clearly identify this entrenchment as delaying the next major advance in machine learning.

astra-6.text:
My worry is less about Transformers themselves and more about what happens when the whole field converges on one approach. Transformers are powerful, and there are good reasons to work on them. But when an architecture becomes dominant, it attracts the compute, the engineering effort, and the research attention. That makes it harder to tell whether alternatives are fundamentally worse or simply less developed.

There’s also a relationship between the algorithms we choose and the hardware we have. We tend to think that we’re selecting the best ideas, but we’re often selecting the ideas that run efficiently on our current infrastructure. And then we optimize that infrastructure further for those ideas. That can become a self-reinforcing cycle.

So I worry about losing diversity in the questions we ask. If trying something different requires resources that only a handful of groups have, a lot of potentially valuable ideas never get a fair test. I want us to keep making progress with Transformers while also making room for approaches that might have very different strengths.

r001.rationale: The response says concentration on Transformers can divert resources and make alternatives harder to evaluate, but it does not identify this entrenchment as delaying the next major advance in machine learning.

sol-6.1.text:
My worry isn’t that Transformers are a bad architecture. It’s that when the field converges so strongly on one approach, it becomes harder to explore alternatives—and harder to tell whether that approach is best or simply the one we’ve invested the most in.

An architecture’s success depends on the ecosystem around it: the hardware, the software, the effort spent making it efficient. Once that ecosystem is optimized for Transformers, a new idea has to compete with all of that accumulated investment. You can end up dismissing something promising because it doesn’t run well on the hardware we’ve built for a different approach.

And that shapes who can participate. If progress means training ever-larger models with ever-larger compute budgets, fewer people can test ideas at the frontier. I want us to preserve room for research that challenges those assumptions—different architectures, different computational budgets, different ways of learning. The concern is allowing today’s success to narrow the questions we ask tomorrow.

r001.rationale: The response says convergence around Transformers makes alternatives harder to explore and may narrow future research, but it does not identify this entrenchment as causing increasing delays in reaching the next major advance in machine learning.
